correctness.rationale: Exact Johnson-graph edge partition into index triples; each mixed triple gives two crossings. Additive pair weights yield a threshold graph; every construction word gives a suffix product bound and exact equality criterion. Centered arithmetic normals with generic perturbation attain the bound. Vertex-avoiding perturbation proves nongeneric upper bound. A standalone integer checker exhaustively verifies words to n=15 and 594 normals through n=35; finite checks corroborate the quantified analytic proof.

evidence: De Loera, Lopez-Campos and Torres (arxiv:2412.12419, Theorem 1.1) give a sharp universal upper bound for arbitrary d-polytopes with N vertices and an algorithm to enumerate sections; the sharpness examples are cyclic polytopes.

Their source concerns broad polytopes and then specific three-dimensional examples and hypercubes. It does not state the hypersimplex-specific sharp formula; in dimension at least four substituting N=binom(n,2) into the general estimate leaves an order-n^4 bound versus the order-n^3 count proved here.
Kaibel and Walter (arxiv:1311.3470, Section 4) establish hypersimplex adjacency but optimize extension complexity, not section vertices.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Neither a general upper bound nor an adjacency characterization implies the exact hypersimplex maximum or all its extremizers without the extra extremal threshold-word argument. All-dimensional stronger dominance was explicitly checked.

evidence: Diaconis, Holmes and Janson (arxiv:0908.2448, Sections 1--2) prove equivalence of additive pair weights and isolated/dominating threshold-graph constructions, and code unlabeled graphs by binary words.

For a construction triple with indices i<j<k, pair-signs equal (b_j,b_k,b_k), so the section problem corresponds to maximizing the number of nonmonochromatic pair-sign triples, not merely to the recognized threshold-graph definition.

value.rationale: Natural all-dimensional exact maximum for a prominent polytope family, a necessary-and-sufficient generic extremal graph classification, and attainment with centroid-passing sections. Its cubic growth is substantially sharper than the available universal quartic bound after substituting the number of hypersimplex vertices. It resolves a complete structural optimization, not a renamed parameter or arbitrary finite slice.
